structure.title: Preface
structure.summary: This letter from HDFC Bank to BSE and NSE provides the Notice of the 31st Annual General Meeting (AGM) and the Integrated Annual Report for FY 2024-25, including the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report. The AGM will be held on August 8, 2025, at 2:00 p.m. IST via two-way video conferencing. The documents are available on the bank's website and are being sent electronically to shareholders with registered email addresses; a letter with web links will be sent to those without. The letter includes company contact details, references a prior intimation dated June 20, 2025, and is signed by the Company Secretary.

structure.title: We understand your world
structure.summary: The section covers HDFC Bank's 31st AGM notice, scheduled for August 8, 2025, via video conference. Ordinary business includes adoption of FY2024-25 financial statements, dividend declaration, reappointment of directors, and appointment of Joint Statutory Auditors with audit fees. Special business includes approval for issuing bonds up to ₹60,000 Crore and appointment of Secretarial Auditors for five years. It also details secretarial information, explanatory statements, regulatory disclosures, annual report availability, e-voting and VC procedures, dividend record date, TDS, document inspection, escrow demat account, member details updation, nomination facility, and dispute resolution via ODR portal.

nodes.title: ORDINARY BUSINESS:
nodes.summary: This notice announces HDFC Bank's 31st AGM to be held on August 8, 2025 via video conference. The ordinary business includes adoption of standalone and consolidated audited financial statements for FY2024-25, declaration of dividend on equity shares, reappointment of directors Kaizad Bharucha and Renu Karnad, and appointment of M/s. B S R & Co. LLP as Joint Statutory Auditors for three years, with continuation of M/s. Batliboi & Purohit for FY2025-26. It also details audit fees of ₹9.90 crore for FY2025-26 and authorizes the Board to finalize related terms and implementation.

nodes.title: SPECIAL BUSINESS:

structure.title: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT PURSUANT TO SECTION 102(1) OF THE COMPANIES ACT, 2013 AND OTHER APPLICABLE PROVISIONS
structure.summary: This section is an explanatory statement under Section 102(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, covering resolutions for HDFC Bank's AGM. It details the reappointment of Mr. Kaizad Bharucha as Whole-time Deputy Managing Director (Resolution No. 4) and Mrs. Renu Karnad as Non-Executive Non-Independent Director (Resolution No. 5), including terms, board recommendations, and interest disclosures. Resolution No. 6 covers the appointment of B S R & Co. LLP as Joint Statutory Auditors for three years, with profiles and fees. Resolution No. 7 proposes raising up to ₹60,000 crore via private placement of bonds, detailing RBI guidelines, board authorization, and use of proceeds. nodes.title: Explanatory Statement for AGM Resolutions 4 and 5
nodes.summary: The page is an explanatory statement under Section 102(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, covering special businesses under Resolution Nos. 7 and 8, with voluntary explanations for ordinary businesses under Resolution Nos. 4 to 6. Resolution No. 4 details the reappointment of Mr. Kaizad Bharucha as Whole-time Deputy Managing Director, originally appointed by Postal Ballot on June 11, 2023 for three years from April 19, 2023 to April 18, 2026, liable to retire by rotation. Resolution No. 5 covers the reappointment of Mrs. Renu Karnad as Non-Executive Non-Independent Director, appointed at the AGM on August 11, 2023 for the period July 1, 2023 to September 2, 2027, also liable to retire by rotation. Both resolutions include Board recommendations, ordinary resolutions, and disclosures of interest by the directors and their relatives.

nodes.title: Resolution No. 6
nodes.summary: Resolution No. 6 details RBI guidelines requiring banks with assets over ₹15,000 crore to appoint at least two joint statutory auditors for three years. It recounts the appointments of Price Waterhouse LLP and Batliboi & Purohit, and the RBI-approved appointment of B S R & Co. LLP for FY 2025-26, with Batliboi & Purohit re-appointed. The Board recommends B S R & Co. for three years (FY 2025-26 to FY 2027-28) subject to RBI approval for remaining years, at the same audit fees as previous year (₹9.90 crore). Profiles of B S R & Co. and Batliboi & Purohit are provided. The Board recommends an ordinary resolution, with no director interest. Resolution No. 7 begins with RBI circulars enabling banks to raise perpetual debt instruments, Tier II bonds, and long-term bonds for infrastructure and affordable housing.

nodes.title: Notice on Appointment of Joint Statutory Auditors and Their Profiles
key_items: Profile of B S R & Co. LLP.
nodes.summary: The page is a notice regarding the appointment of B S R & Co. LLP as Joint Statutory Auditors for three years from FY 2025-26 to FY 2027-28, subject to RBI approval for the last two years. It details the Board's recommendation, eligibility confirmation, and the arrangement with Batliboi & Purohit as joint auditors. It specifies audit fees for FY 2025-26 at ₹9.90 crore, with allocation authority to the Board, and references FY 2024-25 fees in the Directors' Report. It includes profiles of B S R & Co. LLP (founded 1990, converted to LLP in 2013, large staff and partner base, audits listed companies) and Batliboi & Purohit (established 1907, broad service offerings, sector experience, ICAI peer review). It concludes with the Board's recommendation for an ordinary resolution and a statement of no director interest.

nodes.title: Resolution No. 7
nodes.summary: This resolution concerns HDFC Bank's proposal to raise up to Rs. 60,000 Crore through private placement of Long-Term Bonds for infrastructure and affordable housing, Perpetual Debt Instruments (Additional Tier I capital), and Tier II capital bonds over one year from the AGM. It references RBI circulars enabling such issuance and notes the Board's recommendation made on April 19, 2025. Shareholder approval via special resolution is sought under Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013, and it clarifies that a single annual special resolution suffices for NCDs, even if borrowings exceed the Section 180(1)(c) limit. The resolution authorizes the Board to determine terms such as price, coupon, tenor, and listing, with pricing per statutory guidelines, and states that the issuance aims to augment capital, strengthen capital adequacy, enhance long-term resources, and fund infrastructure and affordable housing. It also includes a directors' interest disclosure.

nodes.title: Resolution No. 8
nodes.summary: Resolution No. 8 addresses SEBI Listing Regulation 24A, requiring listed entities to undergo Secretarial Audit by a Peer Reviewed Company Secretary and annex the report to the annual report. It notes the December 13, 2024 amendment mandating shareholder approval for Secretarial Auditor appointment/re-appointment at the AGM. Accordingly, the Audit Committee and Board meetings on April 12 and 19, 2025 recommended appointing M/s. Bhandari & Associates as Secretarial Auditors for five years (FY 2025-26 to FY 2029-30) at an annual audit fee of ₹15,00,000 plus expenses, outlays, and taxes. Bhandari & Associates confirmed eligibility and independence per SEBI Listing Regulations and applicable laws.

nodes.title: Profile of Bhandari & Associates
nodes.summary: The text profiles Bhandari & Associates, a peer-reviewed Practicing Company Secretaries Firm established in 1981, with expertise in corporate secretarial and compliance advisory services across sectors like BFSI, IT, broking, manufacturing, and PSUs, including secretarial audits for Nifty 50 entities. It details the firm's proposed appointment as Secretarial Auditor for the Bank for five years (FY 2025-26 to FY 2029-30), covering compliance checks and record maintenance. Member approval is sought under SEBI Listing Regulations Regulation 24A, with the Board recommending an ordinary resolution (Resolution No. 8) for appointment and remuneration, noting no director or KMP interest.

nodes.title: A Year of Resilience and Steady Progress
nodes.summary: This section reviews HDFC Bank's FY2024-25 Integrated Annual Report, covering the external environment with global GDP growth at 3.3% and India's 6.5% growth amid inflation and policy support. It highlights the bank's resilience and post-merger integration with HDFC Limited, detailing expanded financial services, operational completion, and financial performance: 14.1% deposit growth, 5.4% advances growth, 10.7% PAT rise to ₹67,347.4 crore, NIM 3.48%, and Gross NPAs at 1.33%. Governance improvements, compliance transformation, and Group oversight are discussed, along with CSR impacting over 10 crore lives. Customer experience and technology initiatives including five pillars, GenAI, and biometric onboarding are outlined, plus social value creation, HDB Financial Services' IPO, and a new Independent Director. The Chairman's message emphasizes resilience and stakeholder gratitude.

nodes.title: External Environment and Performance Resilience
nodes.summary: This Integrated Annual Report message from HDFC Bank's leadership covers FY2024-25, addressing stakeholders. It reviews the external environment: global GDP growth slowed to 3.3% amid shifting monetary policies, geopolitical tensions, trade restrictions, and high public debt, creating uncertainty. Despite this, India's economy grew 6.5% with inflation at 4.6%, supported by stable fiscal and monetary policies, regulatory rationalization, budget balancing, lower policy rates, and enhanced liquidity. The report highlights the Bank's resilience, its positioning to benefit from trade realignments, and a positive outlook for India's growth at 6.5% or higher, driven by rural demand, moderating inflation, tax cuts, government spending, and potential private capex recovery.

nodes.title: Merged Strengths
nodes.summary:
Merged Strengths
Two years back we concluded the merger of HDFC Limited into HDFC Bank, bringing HDFC Limited and diverse financial services entities within the Bank’s fold thus transforming the Bank into one of the leading financial institutions of India. The HDFC Bank Group is now a financial conglomerate in the true sense of the term. It now has a sizeable presence in insurance (both life and general), mutual funds, brokerage and alternative investments. FY25 marked the first full year of operations of the combined Group and it now stands strengthened, much bigger in scale, broadened in capability and more unified in purpose. The operational aspects of the integration are now substantially complete. The expansion of home loans across our network, greater choice of Group products to the expanded customer base and a more cohesive branding have contributed to the growth of the Bank, which is at the apex of the Group. As a Group, we have a much broader responsibility to our stakeholders, across the entities.

nodes.title: Financial Performance
nodes.summary: The text reviews the first full year post-merger, highlighting increased balance sheet size, improved asset quality, and the challenge of paring down debt from two differently regulated entities. It notes the HDFC Bank Group's expanded presence in insurance, mutual funds, brokerage, and alternative investments. FY25 faced a monetary policy of 'Withdrawal of Accommodation' constraining credit growth, leading the Bank to recalibrate strategy by increasing deposit proportion and reducing loan-to-deposit ratio. Deposit growth was 14.1%, advances growth 5.4%, PAT rose 10.7% to ₹67,347.4 crore, NIM was 3.48%, and Gross NPAs stood at 1.33%. A dividend of ₹22.0 per equity share was recommended. The Bank has a clear growth roadmap anchored on long-standing values, with the report detailing financial performance and future strategy.

nodes.title: Governance
nodes.summary: The text discusses governance in a post-merger context for a Domestic Systemically Important Bank (D-SIB), covering the transformation of its compliance function to meet enhanced regulatory expectations, commitment to governance, transparency, and regulatory excellence through recalibrated internal systems and technology investments. It highlights community commitment via CSR programs benefiting over ten crore people. Additionally, it addresses strengthened oversight of Group companies (asset management, insurance, investment advisory, etc.) through a dedicated Group Oversight Department reporting to an Executive Director and briefing the Board, ensuring accountability without impeding entity independence.

nodes.title: Customer Experience and Building Technology for the Future
nodes.summary: The text covers HDFC Bank's customer experience strategy, emphasizing customer satisfaction, grievance redressal, and aligning employee incentives. It details digital transformation through five technology pillars, biometric onboarding, and Generative AI. It also discusses social value creation via six focus areas impacting over 10 crore lives, inclusive banking, and Priority Sector Lending. Additionally, it announces HDB Financial Services' successful IPO, making it the fourth listed group entity, and welcomes a new Independent Director. The chairman thanks the government, regulators, employees, and customers, and expresses confidence in future personalized and secure banking.

nodes.title: Technology, Social Value, and Group Milestones
nodes.summary: The page covers the Bank's technology-driven customer journey, spanning five pillars (Journeys, Channels, Core, Data, Security) and advances in GenAI, biometric onboarding, and access to underserved markets. It highlights the social value creation through inclusive banking, organic lending, reduced dependency on Priority Sector Lending Certificates, and six focus areas positively impacting over 10 crore lives. It also announces a milestone for the Group: HDB Financial Services' successful IPO, making the group consist of four publicly listed entities including the Bank.

nodes.title: Banking on What’s Next
nodes.summary: This message from HDFC Bank's Part-time Chairman, Atanu Chakraborty, addresses the challenges of global interdependence and uncertainty, emphasizing the Bank's resilience through its purpose, values, and integrated model. He welcomes new Independent Director Santhosh Keshavan, appointed for three years effective November 18, 2024, and approved by shareholders on January 11, 2025. He thanks the Board, Union and State Governments, RBI, SEBI, and other regulators for guidance. He acknowledges senior management, Group companies, and employees for their dedication, and customers for their support, committing to continuous service improvement. He credits the resolve of colleagues for the Bank's performance.

nodes.title: Balance sheet strength and merger synergies create tailwinds for FY26
nodes.summary: HDFC Bank's FY25 letter reviews macroeconomic conditions—India's GDP growth, inflation, credit growth, and FY26 tailwinds from rate cuts and capital spending—alongside risks. It reports post-merger performance: net profit up 10.7%, balance sheet up 8%, moderated loan growth to cut credit-deposit ratio to 96%, and strong deposit growth. Growth enablers cover technology modernization, digital platforms, analytics, and GenAI; cybersecurity with AI-enabled defense and customer education; customer centricity via service culture, NPS, and branch expansion; people initiatives on attrition, DE&I, and GenAI Academy; ESG through Parivartan CSR and natural resource management; merger synergies with mortgage leadership and cross-sell; subsidiaries and HDB Financial's IPO; and governance. The conclusion expresses optimism, citing merger synergies and deposit mobilization as tailwinds.

nodes.title: Macroeconomic Environment
nodes.summary: The text is a stakeholder letter from HDFC Bank reviewing FY24-25 as a year of consolidation after its merger, noting progress across many dimensions despite global disruptions. It covers the macroeconomic environment: India's average 8.8% GDP growth over three years, FY25 growth moderating to 6.5%, rural demand recovery, elevated inflation moderating urban consumption, and bank credit growth slowing to 11%. It highlights supportive fiscal and monetary measures—RBI's 100 bps rate cuts, government tax cuts, CRR cuts, normal monsoon expectations, and ₹11 lakh crore capital spending—for demand revival in FY26, with RBI forecasting 6.5% GDP growth. Risks include US tariffs, global slowdown to 2.8%, weak consumption rebound, weather disruptions, inflation spikes, market volatility, and geopolitical tensions. It expresses confidence in India's macro fundamentals, low external vulnerability, and sound financial system, positioning India to weather headwinds and become a manufacturing and services hub.

nodes.title: Our Performance
nodes.summary: The text covers HDFC Bank's FY25 performance, the first full year post-merger, reporting 10.7% net profit growth to ₹67,347.4 crore, 13.0% NII growth, and 3.48% NIM. The balance sheet rose 8% to ₹39,10,199 crore, with gross NPAs at 1.33%. Advances grew 5.4% to ₹26,19,609 crore and deposits 14.1% to ₹27,14,715 crore. The bank intentionally moderated loan growth to reduce the credit-deposit ratio from ~110% to 96% and cut high-cost borrowings to 14%. Deposits grew faster than the system, capturing ~14.6% incremental market share. The CEO notes successful merger navigation and targets system-parity advances growth in FY26 and above-system in FY27. Growth enablers are technology, customer centricity, and people. Technology initiatives include modernizing the core, digitizing retail/MSME journeys, scaling platforms like PayZapp, SmartHub Vyapar, Xpress Car Loan, HDFC Bank One, and SmartWealth, launching homegrown digital interfaces with enhanced security and personalization, and investing in analytics and GenAI.

nodes.title: Technology
nodes.summary: The message from the MD & CEO highlights the bank's strong deposit growth, outperforming the system with an 11% market share from only 5% of branches, and an incremental deposit market share of 14.6% in the last fiscal year. It notes successful merger navigation and positioning for faster growth, with loan growth reset and consolidation leading to a stronger bank. The CEO expresses confidence in growing advances on par with the system in FY26 and above it in FY27. Growth enablers identified are balance sheet strength, technology, customer centricity, and people. The technology section details core modernization, scalability, resiliency, the 'Hollow the Core' program, digitization of retail/MSME journeys, real-time credit decisioning, flagship platforms like PayZapp, SmartHub Vyapar, Xpress Car Loan, HDFC Bank One, and SmartWealth, new digital interfaces, analytics investments, and GenAI moving from pilots to a structured platform-driven model with over 15 lighthouse programs. The CEO emphasizes responsible innovation, financial inclusion, and the bank's transformative phase.

nodes.title: Cyber Security
nodes.summary: The text covers the bank's cybersecurity strategy, including investments in advanced AI-enabled capabilities for validation, threat detection, response, and resilience, aligned with global frameworks. It details defense coordination, proactive monitoring, automated incident response, zero-trust, and strategic initiatives like a next-generation CSOC with AI/ML, VAPT, attack surface monitoring, patch management, and email protection. It also addresses customer education and awareness campaigns like 'Vigil Aunty' against phishing and deep fakes, internal training and simulations, and the goal of being a cyber-resilient, compliant, and trusted institution.

nodes.title: Customer Centricity
nodes.summary: The text outlines a customer-centric strategy focused on a 'Service First' culture built on empathy and empowered tools. Digitalization has improved First Time Right service and reduced complaints. The 'Infinite Smiles' NPS program proactively gathers customer feedback as an early warning system. Training and front-line capabilities are emphasized, with service weightage increased in performance metrics. GenAI and AI are being leveraged to enhance customer service speed, consistency, accuracy, and regulatory compliance, while preventing recurring issues. Distribution channels are expanding, with over 700 new branches added in FY 2024-25, totaling 9,455, especially in semi-urban and rural areas, as investments for better community service.

nodes.title: People
nodes.summary: The text highlights employees as the organization's key pillar, covering People initiatives: maintaining flat headcount while sustaining growth, attrition reduction from 26.9% to 22.6%, healthy engagement scores, DE&I and culture transformation impacting over 27,000 managers, sustained gender ratio of 26% (up from 18.09%), leadership development with 500% coverage increase, reskilling/upskilling via role-based learning, a GenAI Academy with tiered proficiency, and employee wellness programs including Inner Harmony, mindfulness, stress management, and counselling. It concludes with a commitment to continuous improvement toward a future-ready organization.

nodes.title: Environmental, Social and Governance
nodes.summary: The text covers HDFC Bank's ESG commitment, including sustainable practices, governance, and stakeholder value. It highlights decade-long CSR via Parivartan, impacting 10 crore people across India, with HRDP in 6000+ villages and new Natural Resource Management focus. The merger's first full year brought a leading mortgage business, cross-sell opportunities, and CASA account growth. It notes governance, group subsidiaries, HDB Financial's IPO, and economic optimism despite global headwinds. The CEO thanks colleagues, board, regulators, and customers, reaffirming commitment to excellence.

nodes.title: Bank Merger Synergies, Natural Resource Management, and HDFC Group Governance
nodes.summary: The page covers the Bank's new Natural Resource Management focus on renewable energy, waste management, afforestation, and soil/water conservation, benefiting communities through partner and colleague efforts. It discusses the first full year post-merger, highlighting the HDFC Bank Group's subsidiaries in insurance, mutual funds, and brokerage, and the mortgage business's growth as the country's largest, driving cross-sell with over 95% of incremental home loan customers opening CASA accounts and half opting for additional products. Governance topics include merger synergies, reduced credit deposit ratio, and deposit mobilization as tailwinds, with a cricket analogy of taking singles to prepare for boundaries. The HDFC Bank Group's commitment to performance and governance standards is reaffirmed, along with HDB Financial Services' successful IPO.

nodes.title: Conclusion
nodes.summary: The conclusion expresses optimism about the Indian economy as the fastest-growing large economy despite global headwinds. It highlights tailwinds for HDFC Bank from merger synergies, reduced credit-deposit ratio, and large-scale deposit mobilization, using a cricket analogy of taking singles and now aiming for boundaries. The CEO thanks colleagues for their passionate service, customers for their support and brand belief, and extends gratitude to the Board, regulators, and stakeholders. It has 9,455 branches, with 51% in semi-urban and rural areas, plus overseas branches for NRIs. The distribution network includes Business Correspondents, ATMs, Cash Recycler Machines, and merchant services. The merger with HDFC Limited enhances geographic coverage. nodes.title: Measuring Meaningful Impacts
nodes.summary: HDFC Bank's materiality assessment identifies and prioritizes sustainability issues critical to business and stakeholders. In FY 2023-24, it adopted a double materiality approach per GRI Universal Standards 2021, evaluating financial relevance and broader impacts. From 16 topics identified in FY 2022-23 via stakeholder engagement and benchmarking, it reassessed impact significance, likelihood, and strategic relevance, refining to 14 topics (9 positive, 5 negative). The process includes identification of material topics, weighted prioritization using stakeholder surveys, evaluation of positive and negative impacts, integration into risk management (mapping 9 opportunities and 5 risks), and sign-off of the materiality matrix by the Board. The assessment ensures alignment with stakeholder expectations and sustainability goals.

nodes.summary: The text presents HDFC Bank's materiality matrix, listing topics such as climate change, sustainable finance, economic performance, compliance, sustainable procurement, corporate governance, customer privacy, systemic risk, financial inclusion, community wellbeing, digital leadership, asset quality, customer satisfaction, and employee practices. It defines financial materiality as the planet and society's impact on the bank's financial performance. It then details two material topics: Economic Performance and Compliance. For Economic Performance, it covers GRI topic 201, impacted capitals (Social, Financial, Manufactured, Human), relevant stakeholders, a description of positive impacts from economic upturns, and FY25 performance metrics (total income and profit after tax). For Compliance, it covers GRI topic 2-27, impacted capitals (Financial, Human, Natural), relevant stakeholders, a description of compliance risk and management measures, and FY25 performance showing zero environmental and social non-compliance. A legend explains capital abbreviations.

nodes.title: Economic Performance
nodes.summary: HDFC Bank's Economic Performance section covers seven material topics: Economic Performance, Compliance, Sustainable & Responsible Financing, Corporate Governance and Ethics, Systemic Risk Management, Financial Inclusion, and Digital Leadership. For each, it details GRI references, impacted capitals, relevant stakeholders, and descriptions of positive or negative impacts. FY25 performance metrics are provided, including 2.35 lakh villages served and 51% of branches in semi-urban/rural areas for financial inclusion, 97% digital transactions and 86% digital acquisitions for digital leadership, a 1.33% gross NPA ratio for asset quality, and 24% recycled paper for sustainable procurement. The section also explains management approaches, ESG risk evaluation, and value creation through responsible lending and sustainable sourcing.

nodes.title: Economic Performance (intro)
nodes.summary: This text covers HDFC Bank's materiality assessment for seven topics: Economic Performance (financial growth and value creation), Compliance (regulatory adherence and zero non-compliance), Sustainable & Responsible Financing (ESG integration and green financing), Corporate Governance and Ethics (board independence, anti-corruption, and training), Systemic Risk Management (multi-layered risk strategy and ESG risk assessment), Financial Inclusion (serving underbanked areas), and Digital Leadership (digital transactions and acquisitions). Each topic includes GRI references, impacted capitals, relevant stakeholders, descriptions of impact (positive or negative risks), and FY25 performance metrics, all within the context of the bank's integrated annual report.

nodes.title: Description of Impact
nodes.summary: The text identifies financial inclusion and digital leadership as material topics, detailing their GRI references (418, 203), impacted capitals, and relevant stakeholders. It describes financial inclusion's role in serving underbanked populations across India, outlining opportunities for market expansion, financial stability, and outreach through MSME and rural banking, with FY25 metrics: 2.35 lakh villages served and 51% of branches in semi-urban/rural areas. It also covers digital leadership's impact through mobile/net banking innovation, customer empowerment, and financial inclusion, reporting FY25 performance: 97% digital transactions and 86% digital acquisitions. Stakeholder groups and capital definitions (F, I, M, H, SR, N) are listed.

nodes.title: FY25 Performance
nodes.summary: The text covers four material topics: Financial Inclusion, Digital Leadership, Asset Quality, and Sustainable Procurement. For each, it details management approach, impact description (opportunity, positive/negative impact), and FY25 performance metrics. It identifies GRI topics, impacted capitals, and relevant stakeholders. Financial Inclusion addresses serving underbanked populations, with metrics on villages served and rural branch openings. Digital Leadership focuses on digital banking innovation and customer experience, with digital transaction and acquisition percentages. Asset Quality discusses responsible lending and ESG risk management, with gross NPA ratio. Sustainable Procurement covers environmentally and socially responsible sourcing, with recycled paper percentage. Stakeholders and capital impacts are listed for each topic.

nodes.title: Asset Quality and Sustainable Procurement Value Creation
nodes.summary: The page covers how HDFC Bank creates value through responsible asset quality management and sustainable procurement. It defines GRI topics, impacted capitals, and relevant stakeholders, outlines the reputational risks of weak asset quality, and explains ESG risk evaluation in lending. FY25 performance shows a 1.33% Gross NPA ratio. For sustainable procurement, it describes integrating environmental and social considerations to improve efficiency, reduce waste and carbon footprint, and engage suppliers on human rights and labor practices, with FY25 performance showing 24% recycled paper of total stationery procured. Stakeholder groups and the capital legend are also listed.

nodes.title: FY25 Performance
nodes.summary: The text outlines HDFC Bank's value creation through asset quality and sustainable procurement. It details GRI topics, impacted capitals, and stakeholders. For asset quality, it describes responsible loan lifecycle management, monitoring for financial stability, and reputational risks from weak asset quality, including a domino effect on lending and the financial system. ESG risk evaluation guides lending decisions. FY25 gross NPA ratio is 1.33%. For sustainable procurement, it covers integrating environmental and social considerations for efficiency, waste reduction, and cost savings; ESG policy collaboration with suppliers on waste, carbon footprint, and human rights; and sourcing recycled, eco-friendly, energy-efficient, local products. FY25 recycled paper is 24% of stationery. Stakeholders listed: customers, employees, vendors, government, investors, community. Capitals defined: financial, intellectual, manufactured, human, social, natural.

nodes.title: Customer Privacy and Data Security
nodes.summary: The text covers two sections. First, Customer Privacy and Data Security (GRI 418): HDFC Bank's robust information security and data protection measures aligned with BCSBI codes, overseen by a Board-level IT Strategy Committee; FY25 performance of zero data breaches; impacts of cyber and data risks mitigated through dedicated policies and independent internal audit assurance; and 100% eligible employee cybersecurity training, with stakeholders listed. Second, Customer Satisfaction (GRI 417, 418): customer-centric approach prioritizing personalized experiences; FY25 Net Promoter Score of 70; value creation through satisfaction surveys (28 lakh feedback captured), adherence to RBI customer rights and grievance policies, and multiple support channels, with stakeholders and capitals impacted specified.

nodes.title: Customer Satisfaction
nodes.summary: The text covers HDFC Bank's customer satisfaction material topic, detailing GRI topics 417 and 418, impacted capitals (Social, Intellectual, Human), and relevant stakeholders. It emphasizes a customer-centric approach focused on excellent service, personalized experiences, and efficient solutions to exceed expectations. FY25 performance shows a Customer Satisfaction Score (NPS) of 70. Value creation includes gathering feedback through surveys, adhering to RBI's Customer Rights and Grievance Redressal policies, and offering multiple channels like 24/7 support and intelligent service options. It reports 28 lakh feedback instances captured across key channels and product journeys, and lists stakeholders including customers, employees, vendors, government, investors, and community.

nodes.title: Employee Practices
nodes.summary: This text covers Employee Practices aligned with GRI topics 2-7 and 401-410, impacting human capital and involving stakeholders like customers, employees, vendors, government, investors, and community. It highlights the bank's belief in people as the cornerstone of success, employee engagement activities, codes and policies, benefits, and proactive human capital enhancement. FY25 performance shows 26.13% women in the workforce. The impact description notes positive outcomes from annual surveys, equal opportunity employment, diversity and inclusion, comprehensive benefits, and training via the MPower platform. The target is 27% women by FY27, with initiatives detailed in the Social-People chapter. It also mentions the Healthy Workplace Award 2024 (Gold Level) and lists capital impacts: Financial, Intellectual, Manufactured, Human, Social and Relationship, Natural.

nodes.title: Community-wellbeing
nodes.summary: This text covers community wellbeing as a material topic with GRI references 203-1 and 413, impacting natural and social/relationship capitals. It outlines stakeholder groups (customers, employees, vendors, government, investors, community), the Bank's core value of building stronger communities through local partnerships and a Board-level CSR & ESG Committee, alignment with government programs, FY25 CSR expenditure of K1,068 crore, and the 'Parivartan' CSR brand empowering disadvantaged sections for self-reliance. It notes multiple targets detailed in the Social-Communities chapter and reports 10.56 crore beneficiaries, followed by a legend of capitals and an Integrated Annual Report 2024-25 page reference.

nodes.title: Climate Change
nodes.summary: HDFC Bank addresses climate change as a material issue, tracking carbon footprint since 2010 and targeting carbon neutrality in own operations by FY32. It reports FY25 GHG emissions (0.59 million tCO2e), energy intensity (5.96 GJ/K crore), GHG emissions intensity (1.05 tCO2e/K Cr), renewable energy consumed (3.22%), and energy consumption (2.06 million GJ). The bank implements TCFD recommendations, conducts climate risk assessments, and integrates sustainability into operations and credit analysis. Stakeholders include customers, employees, vendors, government, investors, and community. It also details impact valuation for financial inclusion (2.35 lakh villages, 51% semi-urban/rural branches, 4.4% increase in rural households with access) and customer privacy/data security (zero data breaches, 100% employee training, NPS of 70 from 30 lakh customers surveyed).

nodes.title: Future-Ready Strategies for Enduring Impact
nodes.summary: This text outlines HDFC Bank's post-merger strategy for FY 2024–25, emphasizing consistent, risk-adjusted profitable growth through four levers: people, customers, technology, and group power, supported by robust governance and risk management. It details priorities like people capabilities, customer centricity, technology excellence, and group synergy, and lists ten strategic pillars including wealth management, digital marketing, branch engagement, payments, corporate and rural clusters, retail and mortgage assets, customer service, compliance, risk management, zero-paper operations, and people development. It also highlights India's resilient economy, the bank's distribution strength, employee behavior architecture (Nurture, Care, Collaborate), digital adoption, and the merger's enhanced ability to offer comprehensive financial solutions for sustainable growth.

nodes.title: Strategic Imperatives
nodes.summary: The text outlines HDFC Bank's strategic imperatives: a service-first, customer-lifecycle-centric approach using AI-driven next-best-action conversations; micro-market-focused multi-format distribution (branches, Smart Banking Lobbies, DBUs, BCs) with profitability tracking; distribution network stats (9,455 branches, 21,139 ATMs/CRMs, 4,150 cities/towns, 51% semi-urban/rural); customer lifecycle engagement via branch network, analytics, and Generative AI/account aggregator plans; digital-led service improvements (priority servicing, Insta Service Journeys, Mobile-first, Aadhaar, Walk Out Working, new Net/MobileBanking); rural growth levers (Vishesh Banking, Bank on Wheels, financial literacy, Samman Samaroh, FPO/MSME partnerships); people capability building (Nurture, Care, Collaborate); and Virtual Relationship Management (VRM) with three pillars—Virtual Relationship, Virtual Sales, Virtual Care—supported by Video KYC, EVA chatbot, multilingual IVR/Voice BOT, trained talent, and secure analytics-led systems.

nodes.title: Government and Institutional (G&I) Business
nodes.summary: The text covers HDFC Bank's Government and Institutional Business growth in FY 2024-25. Key pillars include market leadership in agency business with top rankings in tax collections and new sourcing under the Senior Citizens Savings Scheme, with market shares for GST, customs, and direct taxes. It leverages its distribution network to deepen reach, partnering with district, local, and state bodies for digitalization, tax collection, land monetisation, and online tenders/auctions. The Bank disbursed over ₹90,000 crore to beneficiaries under central schemes, with 12% YoY growth. It enhanced pensioner services via SPARSH and digital life certificates, earning DoPPW recognition. It supports startups with new initiatives, entered cross-border payments aggregation, and launched GIGA for the gig economy. Future plans include expanding digital footprint and customized solutions.

nodes.title: Wealth Management
nodes.summary: HDFC Bank's Wealth Management FY2024-25 covered expanding services across client segments (Ultra-HNW to Mass Affluent) with over 1,000 sales/service experts and 100+ investment analysts. It won 'India's Best for HNW' at Euromoney Private Banking Awards 2025 and Best Private Bank in India at Global Private Banking Awards 2024. 87% of clients generated positive alpha (median 2.6%). Training partnerships with IIM Ahmedabad and Bangalore groomed talent. Service First culture led to an NPS of 87. The bank grew market share via 100+ investor education initiatives, especially in tier II & III cities, and tailored offerings: doubled products for Ultra-HNW, Wealthfy reports for Super-Affluent, and SmartWealth digital platform for Mass Affluent (6 lakh downloads, 4 lakh onboarded). Technology transformation included Shift Right strategy, core banking migration, IMPS Inwards deployment under Lighten the Core, new net/mobile banking platforms, Enterprise Data Lake, API orchestration, BaaS groundwork, Zero Trust security, and structured GenAI adoption for enterprise use cases.

nodes.title: Digital Marketing
nodes.summary: HDFC Bank's digital marketing strategy is a transformation engine building a data-led ecosystem to influence, educate, transact, and retain customers. It covers social media (21 lakh followers, Vigil Aunty influencer with 8 lakh WhatsApp followers, moment marketing, reels/video for service simplification, 56% brand love growth); website as intelligent front door (146 crore visits, 19 crore AEM form visits, mobile-first design, interactive explainers, personalized nudges, live support); analytics using cloud AI/ML for hyper-personalization, campaign precision, funnel fixes, and intelligent service; digital sales via cross-functional PODs achieving 20-45% unassisted channel contribution across core products, with AI/ML-optimized performance marketing; and advocacy through query resolution, testimonials, and online reputation management, all underpinned by IT governance and data security. Future focus includes video, voice, vernacular, and virtual handholding to become India's most loved, trusted digital-first bank.

nodes.title: Payments Business
nodes.summary: HDFC Bank's payments business strategy leverages India's vibrant economy, offering end-to-end solutions for issuing and acceptance across geographies. It leads in credit cards with over 2 crore customers and 5 lakh monthly issuances, commercial cards for businesses, debit cards with 5 crore cards and 3x industry spend, and prepaid cards. The acceptance business includes POS, UPI QR, and the Vyapar app serving 30 lakh merchants. Digital innovations include MyCards (3.5 crore customers), Vyapar merchant app (19 lakh merchants), PayZapp 2.0 (1.6 crore registrations), and SmartGateway. The bank also focuses on consumer finance, digital strategy with new MobileBanking/NetBanking platforms, conversational AI, and ChatBanking on WhatsApp for enhanced customer experience.

nodes.title: Retail Assets
nodes.summary: The text covers HDFC Bank's retail assets strategy, highlighting its top-two market position in personal finance through secured and unsecured lending. It emphasizes sustainable growth, asset quality, and a comprehensive product range for personal and business needs. The strategy focuses on enhancing digital offerings, including unassisted sourcing via Xpress loans and Gold Loan, and introducing a new workflow system for Gold Loan. It details customer acquisition, a centralized GenAI platform for security and compliance, leveraging the existing customer base through branch and virtual channels to reduce costs and improve Cost to Income Ratio, and robust analytics and risk management with prudent pricing.

nodes.title: Mortgage Assets
nodes.summary: The text discusses HDFC Bank's merger with HDFC Limited, creating one of India's largest home loan portfolios. It highlights expanded branch networks, partnerships with Business Correspondents and Facilitators for deeper penetration and financial inclusion, and leveraging digital touchpoints and technology to offer best-in-class home loans. The bank maintains low delinquency levels with robust risk management and aims to expand in semi-urban and rural areas while leading in urban markets. Cross-selling strategies include offering deposits, consumer loans, credit cards, and wealth advisory products, with savings accounts for new home loan customers rising to over 95%. Focus on self-employed categories has increased through new product baskets and surrogate programs. Gross retail mortgages grew to ₹8,35,656.46 crore from ₹7,74,406.33 crore. The bank is positioned to meet strong long-term housing demand in India with world-class service.

nodes.title: Commercial and Rural Cluster
nodes.summary: The text describes HDFC Bank's Commercial and Rural Cluster and Corporate Cluster. The Commercial and Rural Cluster serves MSMEs, microfinance groups, farmers, healthcare, equipment, and transport companies, aiming to support MSME growth through credit and financial solutions. It addresses challenges like credit access, borrowing costs, and collateral constraints, and contributes to Priority Sector Lending (PSL). Goals include increasing PSL lending, growing the book, and generating income while maintaining portfolio quality. PSL lending is 40.4% of the total book net of PSLC, with organic book at 41.7%. The Bank has a strong MSME presence, leading in 14 states and top 3 in 21, and is building district-level leadership. It pursues agricultural financing, with a presence in 2.35 lakh villages, and holds the number one position in transportation finance. Digitalization and risk management are key enablers. The Corporate Cluster serves large businesses, MNCs, manufacturing and service companies, public sector enterprises, and financial institutions, offering holistic engagement including credit, working capital, term loans, cash management, supply-chain integration, trade financing, and payment solutions. The book is well-diversified with average rating AA to AA+. Growth drivers include liability strategy, supply chain financing, trade, investment banking, and fee income improvement. The Bank focuses on deepening client engagement through digital channels, new-to-bank acquisitions, and a client-first approach.

nodes.title: Corporate Banking Strategy: Clusters, Ecosystems, and Client Engagement
nodes.summary: The page covers HDFC Bank's corporate banking strategy, focusing on the Corporate Cluster and Corporate Ecosystem. The Corporate Cluster serves diverse clients including large businesses, MNCs, manufacturers, service companies, public sector enterprises, and financial institutions. It offers holistic engagement through credit, working capital, term loans, cash management, supply-chain integration, trade financing, and payment solutions. The Bank emphasizes relationship-based approach, pricing discipline, selective exposure, and a diversified book rated AA to AA+. The Corporate Ecosystem details stakeholders: clients (digital channels, NTB initiatives, focus clients), shareholders (dividends), government (statutory payments), channel (supply chain finance), employees (salary, empanelment), and balance sheet support. It also covers suppliers/dealers, cash management, cross-border vendors, trade, digital/API/H2H integrations, and a liability strategy to increase wallet share and new-to-bank acquisitions.

nodes.title: Key Growth Drivers
nodes.summary: The text outlines HDFC Bank's key growth drivers, including liability growth through corporate groups and vendor reciprocity, supply chain financing with technology platforms, trade initiatives, investment banking, and fee income improvement. It details digital transformation for corporate banking, employee and customer experience enhancements, and ERP integration. The bank's entry into construction finance for residential and commercial properties, conversion to Lease Rental Discounting, and structured off-balance sheet solutions are covered. The Supply Chain Finance platform's underwriting and onboarding capabilities are highlighted. Realty Finance Business post-merger is discussed, including construction finance, rental discounting, market share, geographic expansion, and cross-selling opportunities, with a focus on technology and customer-centricity.

nodes.title: Favourable Growth Landscape
nodes.summary: The text covers India's favourable banking growth in FY2024-25 due to stable politics and supportive policies, with stronger balance sheets but deposit challenges and liquidity constraints, leading to moderated credit growth. It notes improved profitability and record-low NNPAs, plus rising demand for digital banking. It then discusses global economic uncertainty from US tariffs, geopolitics, and inflation, with IMF downgrading growth forecasts. India's GDP is projected to grow 6.5% in FY2025-26, supported by rural demand, inflation moderation, tax cuts, and government capex. Finally, it details HDFC Bank's response: stress testing for risks, investments in talent and technology, and robust cybersecurity and data privacy initiatives including CSOC, AI/ML, zero-trust architecture, and compliance with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act.

nodes.title: Growing Emphasis on Sustainable Financing and Climate Risk Management
nodes.summary: The Bank advances climate risk management at project, portfolio, and organizational levels, with details in climate disclosures. It highlights climate finance, ESG integration in underwriting, monitoring and verifying operational carbon emissions, and compliance with BRSR and SEBI regulations. Climate risk disclosure gaps are noted, along with COP29 and regulatory pushes for sustainability frameworks. For financial inclusion, the Bank serves rural and semi-urban areas, supports government schemes like PMJDY, PMJJBY, PMSBY, APY, PM SVANidhi, PM Vishwakarma, PMMY, and PMAY Urban 2.0. It aligns CSR skill development with RBI's NSFI, runs financial literacy programs, and uses mobile apps and Micro-ATMs for last-mile access.

nodes.title: Strengthening Resilience
nodes.summary: The section covers HDFC Bank's risk management framework, including governance by the Board, RPMC, and Risk Management Group, and the Three Lines of Defence model. It details the Enterprise Risk Management policy, risk appetite, ICAAP, stress testing, and monitoring. Key risks addressed are credit, market, liquidity, operational, model, cybersecurity, technology, compliance, and reputational risks. Mitigation strategies for each risk are outlined, such as policy formulation, limits, portfolio reviews, and compliance testing. Technology-driven automation and model validation are emphasized. Strategies and capital impacts (Financial, Intellectual, Manufactured, Human, Social/Relationship, Natural) are noted for each risk type.

nodes.title: Control
nodes.summary: HDFC Bank's risk management framework is embedded across operations, evolving with technology and governance. It covers risk appetite, policies, compliance, ICAAP, stress testing, monitoring, and reporting. Governance involves the Board, RPMC, and Risk Management Group, with a Three Lines of Defence model (business units, independent risk/compliance, internal audit). Risks addressed include credit, market, liquidity, operational, model, cybersecurity, technology, compliance, and reputational risks. The ERM policy guides risk appetite, stress testing, and capital planning. Credit risk mitigation involves policy formulation, limits, and portfolio reviews; compliance risk is managed via a board-approved policy, monitoring, and testing. Technology automates risk processes and validates models. Non-financial risks are emphasized.

nodes.title: Risk Management: Technology, Credit and Compliance Risk Oversight
nodes.summary: The page covers technology-driven automation of risk management for efficiency, accuracy, control, and audit trails, while acknowledging technology's inherent risks. It describes independent model fairness validation. Credit risk is managed via the ERM policy, risk appetite, stress testing, ICAAP, and scenario assessments focused on geopolitical, macroeconomic, and sectoral risks. Credit Risk Management sets policies, limits, and portfolio reviews, with oversight of credit strategy and underwriting, aiming for healthy asset quality and optimal risk-reward. Compliance risk covers legal and regulatory sanctions; mitigation includes an annual board-approved compliance policy, active tracking, internal controls, self-certifications, monitoring, and compliance testing, with the strategy of operating strictly within regulations. Capitals impacted are listed as FISRN with a legend.

nodes.title: Strategies
nodes.summary: The text outlines the bank's risk management approach, emphasizing technology-driven automation for efficiency, accuracy, control, and audit trails, while acknowledging technology risks. It details the Enterprise Risk Management framework covering risk appetite, stress testing, capital adequacy, and ICAAP, with a focus on emerging geopolitical, macroeconomic, and sectoral risks. Key risks covered include: Credit Risk—defined as borrower default, mitigated through policies, limits, portfolio reviews, and oversight of credit strategy; Compliance Risk—legal/regulatory sanctions, mitigated by a board-approved policy, monitoring, self-certifications, and compliance testing; Market Risk—adverse market variable changes, mitigated by board-approved policies, limits, portfolio assessments, and counterparty margining; and Operational Risk—inadequate processes, people, systems, or external events, mitigated via a three-line defence system. Strategies and capital impacts (Financial, Intellectual, Manufactured, Human, Social/Relationship, Natural) are noted for each risk type.

nodes.title: Market and Operational Risk: Mitigation and Strategies
nodes.summary: The page covers Market Risk (potential loss from adverse market variable changes affecting financial instruments like money market instruments, debt securities, equities, foreign exchange, derivatives) and Operational Risk (loss from inadequate/failed processes, people, systems, external events; includes legal risk, excludes strategic/reputational). For Market Risk, mitigation includes Board-approved policies, controls, risk limits, portfolio assessments, counterparty risk management, margining; strategies focus on optimizing profitability within liquidity and risk appetite. For Operational Risk, mitigation follows a Board-approved policy with a three-line defence system (business line, ORMD, Internal Audit); strategies minimize operational losses through risk mitigation. Capital impacts are indicated (Financial, Human, etc.).

nodes.title: Strategies
nodes.summary: The text covers Market Risk, defined as potential loss from adverse market variable changes affecting financial instruments like money market instruments, debt securities, equities, foreign exchange, and derivatives. Mitigation includes Board-approved policies, controls, risk limits, portfolio assessments, risk reduction, counterparty risk management for structured products, and margining frameworks. Strategy focuses on optimizing profitability of marked-to-market products within liquidity and risk appetite constraints. It then covers Operational Risk, arising from inadequate processes, people, systems, or external events, including legal risk but excluding strategic and reputational risks. Mitigation involves a Board-approved policy and a three-line defence system (business line, ORMD, Internal Audit). Strategy is minimizing operational losses through risk mitigation. Capital impacts are indicated as Financial and Human.

nodes.title: Climate Risk
nodes.summary: The text covers climate risk, detailing physical and transition risks, mitigation efforts including financing environmentally friendly technologies, ESG integration, and sustainable finance. It outlines strategies for assessing climate transition risk for wholesale and retail portfolios, capacity-building, and financed emissions disclosure. It also addresses liquidity risk, defining it and describing mitigation through Asset Liability Management policy, cash flow monitoring, Basel III ratios, and intraday liquidity frameworks. Strategies include maintaining liquidity buffers, competitive funding costs, and derivative transactions. Capitals impacted are noted for both risks.

nodes.title: Liquidity Risk
nodes.summary: The text covers climate risk and liquidity risk management. Climate risk is divided into physical risks (losses from extreme weather and chronic environmental changes) and transition risks (adjustment to a low-carbon economy, including stranded assets). Mitigation includes financing environmentally friendly technologies and low-carbon infrastructure through ESG integration, sustainable finance, and portfolio emissions. Strategies involve enhancing methodologies for wholesale borrowers, exploring a retail portfolio-at-risk framework using NATCAT scores, conducting capacity-building programs, and disclosing financed emissions. Liquidity risk is defined as the inability to meet financial obligations without unacceptable losses. Mitigation includes an Asset Liability Management policy, cash flow mismatch monitoring, Basel III ratios, intraday liquidity management, and interest rate risk assessment. Strategies include maintaining healthy liquidity buffers (LCR/NSFR), competitive cost of funds, and using derivatives for interest rate management. Capitals impacted are listed.

− Proactive risk assessment and monitoring

nodes.title: Technology Risk
nodes.summary: The text covers Technology Risk, including risks from IT system use, ownership, operation, vendor involvement, adoption, business continuity management, and third-party risk management. Mitigation involves an IT Risk framework with policies, procedures, templates, and assessments for technology risk, vendor risk, business continuity, evaluation of new IT solutions, third-party vendors, outsourced IT, and related services. A Business Continuity Management framework and programme are deployed enterprise-wide. Strategies include aligning business and IT strategies for service availability and customer experience, and advancing technology transformation initiatives. Capitals impacted are Financial, Intellectual, Social and Relationship, and Social and Relationship (FSRI, SR).

nodes.title: Cyber and Data Risk*
nodes.summary: The text covers cyber and data risk, detailing cyber-attack risks like hacking, phishing, and ransomware, and data privacy risks from inadequate controls or non-compliance. It outlines mitigation through the Identify, Prevent, Detect, Respond, Recover framework and lists controls such as firewalls, DLP, DMARC, zero-trust, XDR, and SOC. It describes governance via incident management, policies, crisis plans, and AI-powered SIEM/SOAR with threat intelligence. It mentions ASM, IAM, standards compliance (ISO 27001, ISO 22301, PCI DSS), and a Data Privacy program led by a DPO with privacy by design and ten principles. Strategies include committee governance, mitigation measures, and awareness programs, with a note on capitals impacted (Financial).

nodes.title: Risk of spill-over from Subsidiaries
nodes.summary: The text addresses the risk of spill-over from subsidiaries, defining it as uncertainties or adverse events affecting the holding company's operations, finances, reputation, or strategy. It outlines mitigation measures: subsidiary boards and risk committees manage their own risks, while the Group Risk Management Committee and Group Risk Council review material risks and provide guidance. Group stress testing integrates subsidiary stress tests, and capital adequacy projections incorporate subsidiary business and capital plans. Strategies include group-level oversight of key risks, using subsidiary stress test outputs for group stress testing, and including subsidiary business plans and capital projections in group capital adequacy projections.

nodes.title: Model Risk
nodes.summary:
Model Risk
Risk arising from the use of models, which is the potential for adverse consequences from decisions based on incorrect or misused model outputs and reports.
Mitigation
A well-defined, Board approved Model Risk Management Policy, along with a robust framework including pre-deployment validation, and periodic monitoring, to capture, manage, and mitigate model risk.
Strategies
− Bank has established an independent Model Risk Management Team within the Risk Management Group to manage Model Risk across the Bank.

nodes.title: Managing Emerging Risks
nodes.summary: The text covers the Bank's management of emerging risks through stress testing beyond standard scenarios, focusing on geopolitical, macroeconomic, and sectoral themes to identify portfolio vulnerabilities and act as an early warning system. It details specific risks: growing geopolitical tensions (Russia-Ukraine conflict, Israel-Hamas war, Israel-Iran conflict, tariff measures) and their impact on global growth, inflation, and energy markets; trade realignment from US reciprocal tariffs and shifting global trade patterns; and volatility in key macroeconomic indicators like inflation, interest rates, currency fluctuations, and GDP growth. The Bank monitors these developments closely, assesses portfolio impacts, and implements mitigation measures, while noting no significant direct impact currently.

nodes.title: Emerging Risk - Geopolitical & Macroeconomic Risks
nodes.summary: The text outlines emerging geopolitical and macroeconomic risks, including global instability, trade disruptions, rising protectionism, economic headwinds, and policy uncertainty. It details enterprise-wide mitigation through proactive risk identification, continuous scenario assessment, and monitoring of developments. It lists impacted capitals, specifically financial, and presents strategies such as stress testing focused on geopolitical, macroeconomic, and sectoral themes, monitoring the risk landscape, regular Board updates, and proactive portfolio resizing or limit adjustments to preserve resilience. nodes.title: Management Discussion and Analysis Macroeconomic and Industry Developments
nodes.summary: The text reviews India's macroeconomic and industry developments: GDP growth moderated to 6.5% in 2024-25 due to urban demand slowdown, muted fixed investment, slow government spending, and weak FDI from global tariff uncertainty, while rural demand, agriculture, and exports (especially services) supported growth. Supply-side details cover manufacturing slowdown, services above 7%, construction at 9.4%, and agriculture outperformance. Global growth was 3.3%, with US strong at 2.8% but Eurozone, Japan, and UK muted. Outlook for 2025-26 forecasts 6.5% GDP growth, supported by rural and urban consumption, tax cuts, RBI rate cuts (100 bps to 5.5%), government capex of ₹11 lakh crore, and private investment recovery. Inflation eased to 4.6% in 2024-25, expected at 3.7% in 2025-26. Risks include US tariffs, trade disruptions, geopolitical tensions, financial volatility, climate issues, and domestic demand or equity market corrections. India's economy and financial system remain resilient.

nodes.title: Financial Performance
nodes.summary: The text details the Bank's financial performance for the year ended March 31, 2025, highlighting a 6.7% rise in Total Net Revenue to ₹1,68,302.4 crore, driven by a 13.0% increase in Net Interest Income to ₹1,22,670.1 crore, with NIM at 3.48%. Other Income fell 7.33% to ₹45,632.3 crore but grew 8.91% excluding prior-year stake sale gains. Operating Expenses rose to ₹68,174.9 crore due to branch additions, IT spend, staff costs, and DICGC premium, with Cost to Income Ratio at 40.5%. Provisions dropped to ₹11,649.4 crore, Coverage Ratio was 67.9% (specific) and 172.1% (including general), and GNPAs rose to 1.33% with Net NPA at 0.43%. Profit Before Tax grew 24.8% to ₹88,478.1 crore, Net Profit increased 10.7% to ₹67,347.4 crore, Return on Average Net Worth was 14.56%, and Basic EPS was ₹88.29.

nodes.title: 10.7 per cent increase in FY2025
nodes.summary: The text reports a 10.7% increase in FY2025 and details the Bank's financial position as of March 31, 2025: Total Balance Sheet grew 8.1% to ₹39,10,199 crore; Total Deposits rose 14.1% to ₹27,14,715 crore, with Savings Account Deposits up 5.3% to ₹6,30,467 crore, Current Account Deposits up 1.3% to ₹3,14,094 crore, and Time Deposits up 20.3% to ₹17,70,155 crore; CASA Deposits were 34.8% of Total Deposits. Advances increased 5.4% to ₹26,19,609 crore, and the Domestic Loan Portfolio grew 5.2% to ₹25,73,450 crore. The Debt Equity Ratio was 0.74 versus 1.21 previously. Additionally, HDFC Limited's borrowings of ₹2,87,923 crore as of March 31, 2025, have a maturity schedule with about 15% due in each of the two years up to FY27 and the remaining 70% thereafter.

nodes.title: Business Review

International business details branches, representative offices, product strategy, and financial figures. Government, institutional, and start-up partnerships highlight government deposits, tax collection, digitalization, pensioner engagement, university onboarding, and fintech collaborations. It also includes Chitkara University initiatives, tech innovation, SURU market focus, agriculture lending, government schemes, MSME performance, financial inclusion, sustainability, risk management, internal controls, subsidiary performance, and statutory disclosures.

nodes.title: A. Domestic Business comprises the following:
nodes.summary: The text reviews HDFC Bank's domestic business, covering retail banking (assets, personal loans, auto loans, two-wheeler loans, gold loans, mortgages, payments, digital initiatives), distribution channels (virtual relationship banking), mortgage business, third-party products (life, non-life insurance, mutual funds), wealth management, wholesale banking (corporate, MSME, realty finance, investment banking, government business, digital platforms), and treasury operations (foreign exchange, derivatives, bullion, government securities). nodes.title: B. International Business

It describes the customer-centric product strategy with offerings like trade credits and foreign currency term loans, and the gradual expansion at GIFT City. Financial details as of March 31, 2025, show a balance sheet size of US$10.83 billion, with advances at 1.75% and overseas branches' total income at 1.44% of the Bank's totals.

nodes.title: C. Partnering with Government, Institutions and Start–Ups
nodes.summary: The text highlights the bank's progress in government, institutional, and start-up banking. Key points include increased retail government deposits with over 10% market share in 201 districts, top-three ranking in government tax collection, and new sourcing of Senior Citizens Savings Scheme accounts. It facilitated central government fund transfers (11% growth), digitalized financial operations for government entities, disbursements for land acquisition, and integrated with NeSL for eBGs and treasury systems in six states. It launched "Panchayat Kavach" insurance for Gram Panchayats and digitalized district expenditure reporting. Pensioner engagement intensified with enhanced defence pension products, 99% digital life certificate submission, and extended disbursement to non-HDFC accounts. The bank onboarded 42% of universities and notable religious organizations. Digital products received positive feedback: enhanced FarSight Dashboard and GIGA program for gig workers. It collaborates with fintechs for cross-border trade settlements and signed MoUs with start-up ecosystem partners including DPIIT, SINE IIT Bombay, and state missions.

nodes.summary: This text covers HDFC Bank's initiatives and performance across various domains: HDFC Tech Innovators 2024, partnerships (RBI Innovation Hub, Startup India, MeitY AI Mission), semi-urban and rural (SURU) market focus including agriculture lending, government schemes (AIF, PMFME), funding for small and marginal farmers, FPOs, digital interventions (milk procurement, gold loans), social initiatives, MSME segment performance, financial inclusion and literacy efforts, sustainable livelihood initiative, environmental sustainability, people and technology strategies, cybersecurity, service quality and grievance redressal, risk management (credit, market, liquidity, operational, compliance, group, model, climate, stress testing, BCP), internal controls and audit, performance of subsidiaries (HDFC Life, HDBFSL, HDFC ERGO, HDFC AMC, HSL), and other statutory disclosures including board meetings, annual return, frauds, directors' responsibility, auditors, CSR, related party transactions, whistle blower policy, board evaluation, remuneration policy, succession planning, and compliance matters.

It includes the Opinion section, stating that the financial statements give a true and fair view and comply with the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and the Companies Act, 2013. nodes.title: Key audit matters
nodes.summary: The independent auditor's report for HDFC Bank Limited covers the audit of standalone financial statements for the year ended March 31, 2025. It includes the opinion that the statements give a true and fair view in conformity with the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, Companies Act, 2013, and Indian accounting principles. The basis for opinion outlines compliance with Standards on Auditing and ethical requirements. Key audit matters discussed are the identification and provisioning of non-performing advances, detailing the bank's regulatory compliance and audit procedures, and IT systems and controls impacting financial reporting, including testing of IT general controls. Other information, management's responsibilities, and auditor's responsibilities are also addressed.

nodes.title: Auditor's Report: Other Information and Management Responsibilities

nodes.summary: The page outlines the auditor's responsibilities regarding other information in the annual report, stating that the audit opinion does not cover it and that the auditor will read it when available to check for material inconsistencies or misstatements, communicating any issues to those charged with governance. It also details the Board of Directors' responsibilities under Section 134(5) of the Act for preparing standalone financial statements that give a true and fair view in accordance with applicable accounting standards and RBI guidelines, including maintaining accounting records, preventing fraud, selecting accounting policies, making judgments and estimates, and maintaining internal financial controls. Additionally, the Board is responsible for assessing going concern and overseeing financial reporting.

nodes.title: Auditor’s responsibilities for the audit of the Standalone Financial Statements
nodes.summary: The auditor outlines their objectives: obtaining reasonable assurance that the standalone financial statements are free from material misstatement (fraud or error) and issuing an opinion, noting that reasonable assurance is high but not a guarantee. They describe audit procedures: exercising professional judgment and scepticism; identifying and assessing risks of material misstatement, with higher risk for fraud; understanding internal controls and opining on internal financial controls under Section 143(3)(i); evaluating accounting policies and estimates; concluding on going concern appropriateness and related disclosures; and evaluating overall financial statement presentation. They also cover communication with governance regarding audit scope, timing, significant findings, internal control deficiencies, independence compliance, and key audit matters determination and reporting.
