nodes.title: Investments
nodes.summary:
SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
Investments
The RBI, vide its master direction dated September 12, 2023, issued revised norms for the classification, valuation and operation of investment portfolio of banks, which became applicable from April 01, 2024 (herein after referred as ‘revised norms on investments’).

nodes.title: Classification:
nodes.summary: The text covers the classification, accounting, acquisition cost, and valuation of investments under revised and previous RBI norms. Investments are classified as HTM, AFS, FVTPL (with HFT sub-category), and Group Companies, further divided into six groups. It details the basis for each classification based on intent and SPPI criteria, and notes that purchase/sale transactions are accounted on settlement date except equity shares on trade date. Acquisition costs like brokerage and broken period interest are expensed. Valuation rules are provided for FVTPL, AFS, and various instrument types including quoted/unquoted securities, mutual funds, Treasury bills, Security Receipts, InvITs, and AIFs, specifying fair value methods and treatment of gains/losses.

nodes.title: Investment Classification and Acquisition Cost Rules
nodes.summary: The page details the basis of classification for investments, including HTM for held-to-maturity with SPPI, Group Companies for subsidiaries/associates/JVs, AFS for both collecting cash flows and selling with SPPI, and FVTPL for others, with HFT as a sub-category of FVTPL per RBI specifications. It also contrasts the current classification with the previous approach where HTM was for intended-to-hold, HFT for resale within 90 days, and AFS for the rest. Additionally, it covers acquisition cost, stating that costs like brokerage, commission, and broken period interest are recognized in the Profit and Loss Account and not included in the cost of acquisition.

nodes.title: Valuation:
nodes.summary: The text details valuation norms for investments: FVTPL and AFS fair valued individually with gains/losses routed to P&L or AFS reserve; prior AFS/HFT marked to market with aggregation by groups. Quoted investments valued via exchanges, FBIL, FIMMDA, or foreign market data providers. Unquoted government securities and other fixed income/preference shares valued using FBIL/FIMMDA credit spreads; unquoted equity at break-up value (balance sheet ≤18 months old, else ₹1). Mutual funds at NAV; treasury bills, commercial papers, certificates of deposit at carrying cost; security receipts and InvIT units at NAV from issuer; AIF units at NAV or ₹1 if non-compliant. PTCs valued using FIMMDA spreads. HTM and Group Cos. at cost with impairment for non-temporary diminution; debt securities meeting SPPI accrete/amortize premium/discount. Fair value hierarchy (Levels 1-3) defined with Day 1 gain/loss treatment. NPIs provisioned per RBI, with no offset against appreciation, unrecognized income, and no recognition of appreciation.

nodes.title: Disposal of investments:
nodes.summary:
Disposal of investments:
In accordance with the revised norms on investments, Profit / Loss on sale of investments under the aforesaid categories is recognised in the Profit and Loss Account except for equity instruments designated under AFS at the time of initial recognition, in respect of which the gains and losses are transferred from AFS Reserve to the Capital Reserve. Hitherto entire Profit / Loss on sale of investments, were recognised in the Profit and Loss Account. Cost of investments is determined based on the weighted average cost method. The profit from sale of investment under HTM and Group Cos. categories, net- off taxes and transfer to statutory reserve is appropriated from the Profit and Loss Account to “Capital Reserve”, in accordance with RBI guidelines.

nodes.title: Short sale:
nodes.summary: The text covers the Bank's accounting policies: short sale of government securities under HFT, with MTM and profit/loss recognition on settlement date; repo/reverse repo treated as borrowing/lending with interest expense/income; classification of advances into performing/non-performing per RBI guidelines, including sub-standard, doubtful, and loss assets, and upgrades; provisioning details for non-performing advances (specific loan loss, retail provisioning, write-offs, recoveries, fraud loans as loss assets), general provisions for standard assets (including derivatives, gold, unhedged forex, stressed sectors, step-down subsidiaries, overseas branches), contingent provisions for potential slippage, floating provisions for contingencies, country risk provisions per ECGC, and resolution plans for stressed assets including COVID-19 related stress.

nodes.title: Repo Transactions and Advances Classification Guidelines
nodes.summary: The text covers repurchase and reverse repurchase transactions, detailing their reporting as borrowing and lending, and the accounting treatment of borrowing costs as interest expense and revenue as interest income. It also addresses advances classification, including performing and non-performing assets based on RBI guidelines, stated net of various deductions like bills rediscounted and provisions. The classification extends to loans and investments, including overseas branches and derivative overdues, with NPAs further categorized as sub-standard, doubtful, and loss assets, and upgraded to standard per RBI guidelines.

nodes.title: Provisioning:
nodes.summary: The text covers provisioning policies: specific loan loss provisions for non-performing advances based on management assessment and RBI minimums, retail NPAs by product and delinquency, write-offs per bank policy, and full provisioning for fraud loans. General provisions for standard assets, including derivatives and gold, unhedged forex exposures, stressed sectors, step-down subsidiaries, and RBI-specified borrowers; overseas branches at higher of local regulator or RBI. Contingent provisions for potential slippage, floating provisions up to Board-approved limits for extraordinary contingencies, and country risk provisions per ECGC guidelines. Resolution plans for stressed assets and COVID-19 stress per RBI guidelines, including restructuring and compromise settlements. Securitisation and asset transfer accounting: true sale derecognition, profit/loss recognition, unrealized gains, stressed asset sales, and SR investments. Inter-bank participation with and without risk. Fixed assets and depreciation: cost, capitalization, straight-line method, useful lives, leasehold improvements, software amortization, pro-rata depreciation, and capital reserve treatment. Non-banking assets at lower of net book value or realizable value. Impairment assessment. Foreign currency translation for domestic, integral, and non-integral operations, including revaluation and translation reserves. Foreign exchange and derivative contracts revaluation using FEDAI rates and interpolated rates.

nodes.title: Depreciation, Non-Banking Assets, Impairment, and Foreign Currency Translation
nodes.summary: The page details depreciation rates and policies for various asset classes, including leasehold improvements, software, and PoS terminals, with pro-rata depreciation and revision rules. It covers non-banking assets acquired in claims at lower of net book value or realizable value, and impairment assessment at each balance sheet date. It also explains translation of foreign currency items: income/expenditure at transaction or average rates, monetary items at closing FEDAI rates with revaluation in profit/loss, and non-integral operations' assets/liabilities at closing rates with exchange differences in Foreign Currency Translation Reserve until disposal, plus translation of contingent liabilities.

nodes.title: 9. Foreign exchange and derivative contracts
nodes.summary: The text covers foreign exchange and derivative contract accounting: revaluation of trading spot/forward contracts using FEDAI rates, interpolated rates, and derived rates for longer maturities with Refinitiv/Bloomberg data; present value valuation with discounting and P&L recognition; asset/liability classification based on fair value. It details derivative recognition at fair value, hedging strategies, hedge effectiveness assessment, and accounting for non-trading forwards and principal only swaps under AS-11 (spot translation, premium/discount amortization, accrual interest). It explains fair value and cash flow hedge treatment including reserves and recycling. Finally, it addresses provisioning for derivative contracts with non-performing borrowers.

nodes.title: 10. Revenue recognition
nodes.summary: The text covers revenue recognition policies and employee benefits. Revenue recognition details interest income on accrual for standard assets but on realization for non-performing assets; effective interest for PTCs and bought-out loans; constant yield for discounted instruments; dividend when right is established; mutual fund/AIF income on cash basis; loan processing fees when due; syndication fees on milestone completion; gain/loss on loan sell-down per RBI guidelines; guarantee commission, letter of credit commission, locker rent, and credit card fees on straight-line over contract period; other fees when due and reasonably certain; PSLC fees on straight-line over certificate period. Employee benefits include stock-based compensation using intrinsic value until March 2021 and fair value thereafter per RBI guidelines, with Black-Scholes valuation and straight-line amortization; gratuity as a defined benefit plan valued actuarially with gains/losses in P&L; superannuation as defined contribution with 13% (15% for certain employees) of basic salary contributed; and provident fund with 12% employer contribution, part to pension scheme and part to exempted trust.

nodes.title: Stock Compensation, Gratuity, and Superannuation Benefit Accounting
nodes.summary: The text covers ESIS-2022 stock-based compensation, including RSU grants, vesting, intrinsic value method up to March 31, 2021, fair value method from April 1, 2021 under RBI guidelines, Black-Scholes valuation, amortization, forfeiture adjustments, and accounting entries. It details the gratuity defined benefit plan, including eligibility, benefit formula, exceptions for eHDFC and eLKB employees, trust contributions, actuarial valuation using projected unit credit method, and recognition of actuarial gains/losses. It also describes the superannuation plan, where eligible employees receive retirement benefits via salary or defined contribution, with Bank contributions of 13% (15% for whole-time directors and certain eCBoP staff) to a trust, and expense recognition.

nodes.title: Provident fund:
nodes.summary: The text covers provident fund contributions, including employer contributions to pension schemes and exempted trusts, interest shortfall provisions, and actuarial valuation; pension schemes for certain employees, including defined benefit and frozen liabilities; National Pension System contributions as a defined contribution plan; actuarial estimation for debit and credit card reward points; bullion import, trading, and lending operations; segment information disclosure; and lease accounting under AS-19.

nodes.title: Standalone Financial Statements Schedules: Employee Benefits, Reward Points, Bullion, Segments
nodes.summary: The page covers several schedule notes: Pension and Provident Fund, including defined benefit and defined contribution plans, actuarial valuations, and NPS; Debit and credit card reward points provisioned via actuarial estimation; Bullion operations, including imports on back-to-back basis, pricing, Other Income recognition, and borrowing/lending interest; and Segment information disclosure per AS-17 and RBI guidelines. It details treatment of interest shortfalls in exempted trusts, overseas branches' social security contributions, eLKB employees' pension schemes under different compensation structures, and the Bank's limited liability in NPS contributions.

nodes.title: 15. Lease accounting
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting policies: (15) Lease payments for operating leases are expensed on a straight-line basis per AS-19. (16) Basic and diluted earnings per share are computed per AS-20, using net profit and weighted average shares, with dilution from potential equity shares unless anti-dilutive. (17) Income tax covers current tax under the Income Tax Act, 1961 and ICDS, and deferred tax per AS-22, including recognition, measurement, offsetting, and review of deferred tax assets. (18) Provisions, contingent liabilities, and contingent assets are accounted per AS-29, detailing recognition, estimation, disclosure, and non-recognition of contingent assets. (19) Cash and cash equivalents include cash, gold, digital currency, RBI and bank balances, and call money. (20) Share issue expenses are adjusted against Share Premium. (21) Corporate social responsibility expenditure is recognized in the Profit and Loss Account.

nodes.title: Schedules to Standalone Financial Statements: Derivative Policies

The Derivative policy covers governance, market risk limits (position, tenor, sensitivity, scenario P&L, stop-loss, VaR) set by RPMC and Board, daily mid-office monitoring, risk methodologies, and a Board-approved Customer Suitability & Appropriateness policy scoring customers to ensure suitable derivative products. Classification of derivatives book divides it into trading and hedging books per RBI definitions, with trading managed within RPMC-recommended, Board-approved limits. Hedging policy details documentation at inception (hedge relationship, risk objective, effectiveness methods), ongoing effectiveness assessment using qualitative and quantitative methods, hedging book composition, tenor constraints, use of derivatives (including FX forwards) for balance sheet hedging, and accounting treatment: fair value hedge changes in P&L; cash flow hedge effective portions in Cash flow hedge reserve (recycled to P&L with hedged item) and ineffective portions in P&L; and AS-11 treatment for non-trading FX forwards and principal only swaps (not marked to market, translated at spot, premia/discount amortized, interest accrued).

nodes.title: • Provisioning, collateral and credit risk mitigation

It details evaluating counterparty creditworthiness to set limits, stipulating credit covenants as triggers for collateral calls or termination, and using Credit Support Annex agreements with major international and Indian financial institutions for non-centrally cleared forex and derivative transactions. It also states conformance to RBI provisioning guidelines, treating overdue receivables from crystallised positive mark-to-market derivative values as non-performing assets if unpaid for 90 days or more, and making full provision for overdue and future receivables related to non-performing derivative contracts.

nodes.title: I. Key Features and Objectives of Remuneration Policy
key_items: Review of Remuneration Policy of the Bank
nodes.summary: The text outlines the Bank's Remuneration Policy, detailing its alignment with business strategy, market dynamics, and internal complexities. Its objective is to provide a fair, transparent structure to attract and retain talent, designed per sound compensation principles and regulatory requirements. The performance management system holistically assesses employees, differentiating pay based on contribution, performance, skill, experience, grade, and market forces, while integrating compliance and risk management. The NRC ensures compensation adjusts for prudent risk, is symmetric with risk outcomes, sensitive to risk time horizons, and aligns cash, equity, and other forms with risk. It also covers the annual review of the Compensation Policy, including changes based on Audit observations, reviewed and approved by the NRC on March 26, 2025.

nodes.title: II. Design and Structure of Remuneration
key_items: b) Variable Pay – For Senior Management and Material Risk Takers
nodes.summary: The text outlines the design and structure of remuneration per RBI guidelines for FY ended March 31, 2025. It details fixed pay components (base salary, allowances, perquisites, retirement benefits), determinants, and approval processes. Variable pay for senior management and material risk takers includes composition (cash and share-linked instruments like ESOPs), limits (up to 300% of fixed pay, with minimum non-cash portions), deferral (at least 60% deferred over minimum three years), vesting, and malus/clawback arrangements with triggers and a four-year horizon. Approval processes and an addendum for US-listed company clawback compliance are covered. For other employees, variable pay plans include Annual Bonus Plan, Performance-linked Plans, ESOPs, and Restricted Stock Units. It also addresses risk/control staff compensation, guaranteed bonuses, severance pay, hedging prohibition, and statutory bonus.

nodes.title: III. Remuneration Processes
nodes.summary: The text covers remuneration processes including hire fitment based on job size, experience, location, and credentials, with pay ranges subject to market trends and exceptions for critical profiles. Pay increments and revisions are guided by annual salary surveys, internal equity, performance, and retention of critical talent, with specific approval processes for senior roles. It details how current and future risks are considered in fixed pay, variable pay (including PLP plans with deterrents and deferrals, annual variable pay, and malus/clawback clauses), and performance measurement for Whole Time Directors using a Balanced Scorecard framework with parameters like business performance, stakeholder relationship, audit and compliance, digital transformation, people excellence, and strategic initiatives, along with business unit metrics such as revenue growth, profit growth, and cost-to-income improvement.

nodes.title: d) Improvement in Gross NPA over the previous year and

Variable pay plans include: for Sr Vice President I and above, cash variable pay for short-term performance and Employee Stock Options for long-term performance; for Vice President and below, cash variable pay based on annual performance, with FY 2024-25 E3-D3 band units. Annual bonus is a gross salary percentage per job band, using business unit performance, rating, job band, and functional category. Performance-linked Plans (PLPs) for sales, collections, customer service, and relationship roles use balanced scorecards with targets and qualitative moderation, with deferred payouts for unforeseen risks, paid monthly or quarterly.

nodes.title: C. ACCOUNTING METHODOLOGY

It notes separate disclosure for subsidiary policies differing from the Bank's. Additionally, it addresses the use of estimates, requiring management to make prudent and reasonable assumptions for assets, liabilities, income, and expenses, acknowledging that actual results may differ and revisions are recognized prospectively.

nodes.title: D. SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
nodes.summary: The section covers significant accounting policies for investments under revised RBI norms effective April 2024, including classification into HTM, AFS, FVTPL, and Group cos, with six groups. It also addresses non-performing investments, short sales, life insurance investments, and classification and valuation of non-linked investments including debt securities, equity, mutual funds, and AT1 bonds. Additionally, it covers general insurance claims incurred, premium deficiency, acquisition costs, pool fund contributions, income tax, segment reporting, earnings per share, provisions, cash equivalents, share issue expenses, and CSR expenditure.

nodes.title: D. SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (intro)
nodes.summary: This text outlines significant accounting policies for investments, specifically for a bank. It details the revised RBI norms effective April 2024, covering investment classification into HTM, AFS, FVTPL, and Group cos, with HFT as a subcategory of FVTPL, and further classification into six groups. It describes the basis of classification, including SPPI criteria, and contrasts with previous classifications (HFT, AFS, HTM) and shifting rules. It addresses acquisition cost treatment, recognizing brokerage and broken period interest in profit and loss. Valuation methods are explained: FVTPL and AFS fair valued individually, with gains/losses treated differently, and quoted/unquoted investments valued using specified sources like stock exchanges, FBIL, FIMMDA, Bloomberg, and Refinitiv.

nodes.title: Investment Classification, Basis, and Acquisition Cost Summary
nodes.summary: The page details investment classification under revised norms into HTM, AFS, FVTPL, and Group cos, with six groups under each, and notes prior classification and settlement-date accounting. It explains the basis: HTM for held-to-maturity SPPI investments, Group cos for subsidiaries/associates/JVs, AFS for collect-and-sell SPPI investments, and FVTPL for others, including HFT per RBI, with prior basis noted. Acquisition cost covers brokerage, commission, and broken-period interest recognized in profit and loss, not included in cost.

nodes.title: Valuation:
nodes.summary: The text details valuation and disposal policies for investments, including fair value measurement for FVTPL and AFS categories, and methods for quoted and unquoted securities, mutual funds, and other instruments. It covers impairment, fair value hierarchy (Levels 1-3), Day 1 gain/loss treatment, and non-performing investments. Disposal recognition and short sale transactions are explained. Life insurance investment regulations and classification into six groups are outlined, with valuation bases for debt securities, money market instruments, AIFs, security receipts, equity shares, ETFs, InvITs, REITs, and AT1 bonds.

nodes.title: Investment Accounting, Short Sales, and Life Insurance Schedules
nodes.summary: This page presents schedules to the consolidated financial statements as at March 31, 2025, covering three sections. First, it details non-performing investments (NPIs), including RBI-based identification and provisioning, non-set-off of provisions against appreciation, non-recognition of appreciation and income until received, disposal of investments with profit/loss recognition rules for AFS equity instruments and HTM/Group Cos., and cost determination via weighted average. Second, it covers short sale transactions in Central Government dated securities, categorizing short positions under HFT, netting, mark-to-market treatment, and profit/loss recognition on settlement date. Third, it addresses life insurance investments under the Insurance Act, 1938, IRDAI regulations, and recognition at cost including brokerage and taxes but excluding accrued interest.

nodes.title: Classification and valuation of investment (other than linked business) is done on the following basis:
nodes.summary: The section outlines classification and valuation of non-linked investments. Debt securities are grouped into six categories, with held-to-maturity valued at historical cost with straight-line amortization/accretion, and equity shares, ETFs, InvITs, REITs, and AT1 Bonds at fair value based on exchange prices, NAV fallbacks, or CRISIL yields for AT1. Unrealized gains/losses go to reserves, and thinly traded or unlisted securities are valued at cost or NAV, with bonus and right entitlements recognized. Preference shares: redeemable held at historical cost with premium amortization/discount accretion; other listed at fair value using primary/secondary exchange prices within 30 days, with unrealized gains/losses in reserves; unlisted and thinly traded non-redeemable at historical cost with provisions for diminution. Mutual fund section covers accounting policies for mutual funds, insurance investments, advances, securitisation, fixed assets, non-banking assets, impairment, unclaimed policyholder amounts, life and general insurance accounting, employee benefits, and insurance schedules.

nodes.title: a) Debt securities
nodes.summary: The text details the classification and valuation of non-linked investments, covering six groups: Government Securities, Other Approved Securities, Shares, Debentures and Bonds, Subsidiaries/Joint Ventures, and Other Investments. It states that purchase/sale transactions are on trade date and SLB securities remain investments. For debt securities, it describes held-to-maturity valuation at historical cost with straight-line amortization/accretion for government securities, money market instruments, and AIF/Security Receipts. For equity shares, ETFs, InvITs, REITs, and AT1 Bonds, it outlines fair value based on primary/secondary exchange prices, NAV fallbacks, and AT1 valuation using CRISIL yields. It notes unrealized gains/losses in reserves and covers valuation of thinly traded and unlisted securities at cost or NAV, plus recognition of bonus and right entitlements.

nodes.title: c) Preference Shares
nodes.summary: The text outlines valuation methods for preference shares: redeemable preference shares are held to maturity at historical cost with premium amortization or discount accretion. Other listed preference shares are valued at fair value using the last quoted closing price on the primary exchange at the balance sheet date, or secondary exchange if not traded on primary, or the earliest previous day's price if not traded on either, provided it is within 30 days. Unrealised gains or losses are recognized in 'Reserves and Surplus' under 'Other reserves'. Unlisted preference shares (other than redeemable) and thinly traded listed preference shares (other than redeemable) are valued at historical cost with provisions for diminution determined individually.

nodes.title: d) Mutual fund
nodes.summary: This section covers accounting policies for mutual funds, insurance investments, advances, securitisation, fixed assets, non-banking assets, impairment, and unclaimed policyholder amounts. It details valuation methods for securities, classification and provisioning for advances across banking, NBFC, and insurance entities, securitisation and transfer of assets, depreciation of fixed assets, treatment of non-banking assets, impairment assessment, and unclaimed amounts. It also outlines life insurance unclaimed amounts management, general insurance accounting including foreign currency translation and revenue recognition, employee benefit plans (gratuity, superannuation, provident fund) with actuarial valuations, other subsidiaries' benefits and transactions, and insurance accounting schedules for reserves, reinsurance, and claims.

nodes.title: d) Mutual fund (intro)
nodes.summary: This text covers accounting policies for mutual funds, insurance investments, advances, securitisation, fixed assets, non-banking assets, impairment, and unclaimed policyholder amounts. It details valuation methods for various securities, classification and provisioning for advances across banking, NBFC, and insurance entities, securitisation and transfer of assets, depreciation of fixed assets, treatment of non-banking assets, impairment assessment, and unclaimed amounts. The policies are framed under regulatory guidelines and accounting standards.

nodes.title: Life Insurance
nodes.summary: The text outlines the management of unclaimed policyholder amounts in life insurance, referencing the Master Circular and Investment Regulations 2016. It covers: (a) determination of unclaimed liability via NAV, disclosed under 'Other liabilities and provisions'; (b) maintenance of a single segregated fund invested in money market instruments, liquid mutual funds, or fixed deposits, valued at historical cost with straight-line amortization/accretion, disclosed under 'Other assets'; (c) income on unclaimed amounts accreted to the fund on an accrual basis, net of fund management charges; and (d) transfer of amounts unclaimed for 10 years as of September 30, along with accretions, to the Senior Citizen Welfare Fund per IRDAI regulations.

nodes.title: General insurance
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for general insurance unclaimed amounts (deposited to Senior Citizen Welfare Fund after 10 years), foreign currency translation for domestic, integral, and non-integral operations including revaluation and translation reserves, and foreign exchange/derivative contracts including valuation, hedging, and mark-to-market. It details revenue recognition across banking (interest, fees, dividends), life insurance (premiums, reinsurance, linked income), general insurance (premiums, commissions), asset management, stock broking, and other services (commission, dividends, interest). Employee benefits include stock-based compensation (intrinsic value then fair value), gratuity (defined benefit), superannuation (defined contribution), and provident fund (defined benefit for interest shortfall).

nodes.title: Employee Benefit Plans: Gratuity, Superannuation, and Provident Fund
nodes.summary: The text covers employee benefit plans: gratuity, superannuation, and provident fund. Gratuity details include contributions to trusts, benefits for employees of erstwhile Lord Krishna Bank, and specific calculations for HDFC Limited, HDFC Capital Advisors, and General Insurance employees; actuarial valuation using the projected unit credit method per AS-15, with actuarial gains/losses in profit and loss. Superannuation: Bank employees above a prescribed grade receive retirement benefits via salary or defined contribution plan (13% of basic salary, 15% for whole-time directors and eligible eCBoP staff) to a trust; no further liability. Other subsidiaries recognize superannuation contributions as expenses. Provident fund: Bank covered under the Employees Provident Fund Act, contributing 12% of basic salary, with 8.33% to the Pension Scheme and the balance to an exempted trust; interest shortfall made good by the Bank and actuarially valued as a defined benefit plan per IAI guidance. Overseas branches contribute to government social security schemes as defined contribution. Other subsidiaries' employees are covered under the Provident Fund Act.

nodes.title: Other Subsidiaries
nodes.summary: This text covers employee benefit plans including gratuity, superannuation, provident fund, pension, and NPS, detailing contributions, actuarial valuations, and accounting treatments. It also addresses short-term and other long-term employee benefits, debit/credit card reward points, bullion transactions, lease accounting for operating and finance leases, reserve for unexpired risk in general insurance, and policyholders' funds in life insurance with valuation methods and additional reserves. Finally, it covers reinsurance premium ceded and claims paid and incurred for both life and general insurance.

nodes.title: Insurance Accounting Schedules: Reserves, Reinsurance, and Claims

Finally, it describes benefits paid for Life Insurance, distinguishing non-linked and linked business, and accounting for claims, surrenders, withdrawals, lapses, reinsurance recoveries, and repudiated or disputed claims.

nodes.title: II. Claims incurred
nodes.summary: The text covers claims incurred in general insurance, including paid claims, changes in outstanding claims liability, IBNR and IBNER, and settlement costs, with provisioning based on management estimates and actuarial review by the Appointed Actuary per IRDAI guidelines. It also addresses premium deficiency recognition on an annual basis when expected costs exceed unexpired risk reserves. Acquisition costs are defined and expensed as incurred. Contribution to Pool Funds is described, including participation in the Terrorism Pool and Marine Cargo Pool for Excluded Territories, managed by GIC, with cession percentages and provisioning. The text also mentions contribution to the Solatium Fund for motor policies. New Fund Offer expenses and commissions for mutual funds are borne by the Asset Management entity or schemes, in line with SEBI circulars. Finally, income tax expense is detailed, covering current and deferred tax for the Group and overseas subsidiaries, determined under applicable tax laws and AS-22.

nodes.title: Premium Deficiency
nodes.summary: The text describes accounting for insurance claims, including legal expenses, IBNR/IBNER classification, and provisions for outstanding claims net of reinsurance and recoveries. Provisions are based on ultimate amounts, past experience, and settlement costs. Claims are recognized on intimation using surveyor/insured estimates. IBNR/IBNER liabilities are estimated by the Appointed Actuary per IRDAI and Institute of Actuaries guidelines, using accepted methods reviewed periodically. Premium deficiency is recognized annually if expected claim costs, expenses, and maintenance exceed unexpired risk reserves, certified by the actuary.

nodes.title: III. Acquisition costs
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies: acquisition costs expensed as incurred; participation in Terrorism and Marine Cargo Pools for Excluded Territories (Russia, Ukraine, Belarus) with cession percentages and reserve creation; Solatium Fund contributions based on motor premiums; NFO expenses borne by asset management entity, with scheme expenses including commissions borne by schemes from October 2018; income tax including current and deferred tax, recognition of deferred tax assets, and offsetting; segment reporting per AS-17 and RBI guidelines; earnings per share per AS-20; provisions and contingencies per AS-29 including recognition criteria and disclosures; cash and cash equivalents definition; share issue expenses adjusted against share premium; and CSR expenditure recognition.

nodes.title: Statement by the Director Responsible for the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report
nodes.summary: HDFC Bank's Director statement outlines its decade-long sustainability journey since adopting 'Sustainability' as a fifth core value. In FY2024-25, the Bank embedded ESG principles into operations, decision-making, and stakeholder engagement to drive inclusive, resilient growth. Initiatives reduced operational emissions through renewable energy, IT tracking, and energy-efficient equipment. It scaled Sustainable Finance across clean energy, electric mobility, MSMEs, and affordable housing, issuing its first Sustainable Bond in 2024. ESG yardsticks were integrated into credit evaluation, and business teams were sensitized. The Bank supported government flagship schemes in micro-insurance, pensions, MSME funding, digitization, agriculture, and livelihoods. Its CSR program, Parivartan, impacted millions via rural livelihoods, financial literacy, healthcare, education, and skill development. The statement reaffirms commitment to balancing economic well-being with planetary protection through collaboration with partners, regulators, and communities.

nodes.title: HDFC Bank BRSR Independent Assurance Statement Overview
key_items: Intended Users of this Assurance Statement
nodes.summary: SGS India issued an independent reasonable assurance statement for HDFC Bank's BRSR report for FY 2024-25, covering BRSR Core attributes. The reporting framework includes SEBI BRSR Core and reporting guidelines circulars and the Greenhouse Gas Protocol. Intended users are all HDFC Bank stakeholders. Responsibilities: company management is responsible for report information; SGS India expresses an opinion within the defined assurance scope and disclaims responsibility beyond it. Assurance standard: ISAE 3000 (Revised) and ISAE 3410, with evidence-gathering procedures designed for a reasonable level of assurance, not absolute certainty, confirming information is fairly stated and free from material misstatements.

nodes.title: Statement of Independence and Competence

The scope includes assessing BRSR Core KPIs for HDFC Bank and its regional offices in India. Methodology involves desktop review, personnel interaction, site visits, and remote verification, including criteria assessment, data aggregation review, and document verification. Limitations exclude non-scope disclosures, external data, forward-looking statements, and financial data evaluation. Findings conclude that the Core Indicators are complete, accurate, reliable, and BRSR-compliant.

nodes.title: SGS Assurance Statement for HDFC Bank BRSR Report
nodes.summary: The page presents SGS India's assurance statement on HDFC Bank's BRSR report, covering independence, team qualifications, scope, methodology, and limitations. The scope assesses BRSR Core KPIs' quality, accuracy, and reliability for April 2024–March 2025 across HDFC Bank's regional offices in India. Methodology includes desktop review, personnel interaction, on-site visits, remote data verification, criteria suitability assessment, analytical procedures, sample-based document verification, data aggregation review, and critical report review. Limitations exclude non-scope disclosures, data outside operational sites, validation beyond findings, forward-looking statements, product/service information, external sources, expert opinions, strategy linkages, and other framework mappings, with a ±5% uncertainty threshold; financial data assessment is excluded, relying on third-party audited reports.

nodes.title: Findings and Conclusions
